courseDescription: A comprehensive guide to mastering the conventions of scholarly communication. This course transitions learners from general composition to sophisticated, evidence-based academic discourse. You will learn to navigate the rhetorical demands of the academy, construct logically sound arguments using the Toulmin model, refine your prose for clarity and cohesion, and ethically integrate scholarly sources. By the end of the course, you will be able to produce polished research papers and adapt your writing style to various academic genres and disciplines.
targetLearner: Students, early-career researchers, and professionals seeking a concept-first, systematic approach to mastering scholarly writing and research argumentation.

projects.project_description: Throughout this course, you will research, draft, and polish a 1,500-word academic research paper on a topic of your choice. You will progress through the entire scholarly workflow: from developing a research question and a Toulmin-based argument to synthesizing peer-reviewed sources and applying advanced revision techniques.
projects.final_deliverable: A complete, formatted 1,500-word academic research paper including an abstract, an arguable thesis supported by evidence and counterarguments, integrated scholarly citations, and a full reference list.

units.title: The Academic Writing Situation
units.description: This unit establishes the foundational mindset shift required for university-level writing. It moves beyond high-school patterns to treat writing as a scholarly conversation, focusing on audience analysis, critical reading, and the transition from a broad topic to a viable research question.

lectures.title: Purpose and Audience
lectures.description: Transition from general essay writing to the specific demands of the academy by understanding the rhetorical triangle and the conventions of scholarly discourse.

sessions.title: What Makes Writing Academic
sessions.description: This session explores the core characteristics of academic prose, emphasizing inquiry and evidence over mere opinion. You will learn to distinguish between personal expression and scholarly contribution, which is essential for unlearning high-school habits and adopting a professional scholarly identity.
sessions.sessionOutline:
Welcome to the first session of Academic Writing. We begin by dismantling the most common misconception among new scholars: that academic writing is simply 'fancy' writing used to express personal opinions. In a public lecture style, we must first visualize the 'Rhetorical Shift.' On the whiteboard, I draw a line dividing 'Personal Expression' from 'Scholarly Contribution.' I explain that while high school writing often rewards 'knowledge-telling'—where a student proves they read a book by summarizing it—university-level work demands 'knowledge-transforming.' This means using existing information to solve a problem or fill a gap. The core idea here is that the writer is no longer the center of the universe; the inquiry is.

To make this concrete, I use the analogy of a crowded dinner party conversation that has been going on for centuries. You don't just walk in and shout your opinion; you listen to what has been said (the literature), identify a point of disagreement or curiosity (the gap), and then contribute a measured, evidenced response. This 'writing as conversation' metaphor is vital because it shifts the student's mindset from 'performing for a grade' to 'participating in a community.' I will illustrate this on the board by sketching a web of interconnected authors, showing how one paper's conclusion becomes the next paper's introduction. 

We then move to the formal distinctions, specifically the difference between a blog post and a peer-reviewed article. I ask the students to imagine the 'burden of proof.' In a blog post, the author's persona and charisma carry the weight. In a scholarly article, the evidence must stand even if the author is anonymous. I list three pillars on the board: Transparency (showing your work), Skepticism (anticipating counter-arguments), and Precision (using technical language to avoid ambiguity). A common pitfall for students is thinking that 'academic' means 'using big words.' I address this directly by showing how 'big words' are often just masks for weak logic, whereas true academic prose uses specific terminology to achieve a level of accuracy that common language cannot reach.

To test this conceptual shift, I introduce a diagnostic exercise. I present two short texts on the same topic—one a passionate editorial and the other a dry, data-driven abstract. Instead of asking which is 'better,' I ask which one permits the reader to verify the claims independently. This reveals the heart of academic integrity: you are writing for an audience of skeptics, not fans. This exercise exposes if students still value emotional persuasion over logical substantiation. 

I conclude the session by focusing on 'Identity.' Many students feel like imposters when they stop using 'I feel' or 'I believe.' I explain that the 'academic voice' is a professional coat you put on. It’s not about losing your personality; it's about gaining authority through objectivity. I map out a spectrum on the board from 'Opinion' to 'Inquiry-based Argument' to show that the strongest papers aren't the ones with the loudest voices, but the ones with the most undeniable evidence. This sets the stage for the rest of the unit, where we will learn the specific tools to build that authority.

tasks: Identify three key differences between a blog post and a peer-reviewed article on the same topic.
Reflect on a previous writing assignment and categorize it as either 'knowledge-telling' or 'knowledge-transforming'.

sessions.title: Genre and Convention
sessions.description: This session introduces the concept of genre as a patterned response to recurring situations. You will understand how academic conventions serve as a 'handshake' between writers and readers, helping you navigate different departmental expectations with confidence.
sessions.sessionOutline:
Start this session by challenging the common misconception that 'genre' is merely a synonym for 'literary category' like mystery or sci-fi. Instead, use the whiteboard to define genre as a 'social action'—a patterned response to a recurring rhetorical situation. This shift is crucial because it moves students away from seeing academic rules as arbitrary hurdles and toward seeing them as functional tools. Draw a parallel to a handshake: it is a convention that signals mutual understanding and respect. In the academy, specific conventions like the literature review or the citation style are the intellectual 'handshakes' that allow a chemist and a sociologist to recognize valid work within their respective spheres.

Transition into the concept of disciplinary variations. Use a split-screen approach on the whiteboard to contrast how 'evidence' is treated in the humanities versus the hard sciences. For instance, explain why a history paper relies on the interpretative weight of a primary source quotation, whereas a lab report prioritizes the replicability of data trends. This part of the lecture is designed to prevent the 'one-size-fits-all' trap where students try to apply English literature writing styles to their Economics or Biology coursework. By visualizing these differences, we help the learner understand that becoming a good academic writer means becoming a 'rhetorical chameleon' who can adapt to different departmental expectations.

Introduce the 'Implicit vs. Explicit' convention model. Some rules are explicit, such as the use of APA or Chicago style, while others are implicit, such as the level of hedging required when making a claim (e.g., 'the data suggests' vs. 'the data proves'). This is a prime moment for a diagnostic exercise: present the learners with a set of specific conventions and ask them to match these to the corresponding discipline. This exercise isn't just about memorization; it’s about revealing the underlying values of a field—for example, why do scientists use the passive voice to emphasize objectivity, while some social scientists prefer the first person to acknowledge their positionality?

Conclude the session by deconstructing the anatomy of a scholarly abstract. Rather than treating it as a summary, draw a diagram on the whiteboard that identifies the generic components: the problem, the methodology, the findings, and the significance. Explain that an abstract is a promise to the reader. By showing how these components function as a standardized map, students learn to read faster and write more predictably. Use this to lead into the final practice task of the session, where they analyze an abstract to find these 'moves,' grounding the abstract concept of genre into a concrete, repeatable skill for their own research papers.

tasks: Match specific writing conventions (e.g., use of 'I', citation style) to their respective academic disciplines.
Analyze a short abstract to identify its generic components.

sessions.title: Audience and Register
sessions.description: This session focuses on the 'academic register'—the level of formality and tone expected in scholarly work. You will learn to analyze your audience's expertise and adjust your language to meet their expectations, ensuring your arguments are taken seriously by a scholarly audience.
sessions.sessionOutline:
In this concept-first session, we shift our focus from 'what' we are saying to 'how' we are perceived by the scholarly community. I begin by defining the 'Academic Register' not as a list of fancy vocabulary, but as a strategic choice of linguistic tools designed to project objectivity, precision, and humility. On the whiteboard, I draw a spectrum: on one end, 'Intimacy' (personal letters, blogs); on the other, 'Distance/Objectivity' (academic journals). The core idea here is that the academic register isn't about sounding smart; it is about minimizing the distance between the reader and the evidence while maximizing the distance between the reader and the writer’s personal whims. This helps students move past the common misconception that big words equal better writing.

Next, we tackle the 'Expert Audience.' I use the whiteboard to visualize the internal checklist of a scholarly reader. Unlike a general audience who reads for entertainment or a high school teacher who reads to check if a student followed directions, the expert reader is looking for intellectual vulnerability and evidentiary support. I explicitly explain that an expert reader is often a 'skeptic by default.' If a student writes, 'Everyone knows that climate change is bad,' the expert reader immediately asks, 'Who is everyone? How is bad defined? Where is the metric?' By introducing this 'skeptic on the shoulder' metaphor, I teach students to anticipate these objections and adjust their register—moving from assertive, colloquial generalizations to cautious, qualified claims (hedging).

To bridge the gap between intuition and application, I conduct a 'Live Deconstruction' on the board. I write a sentence full of first-person pronouns, emotional intensifiers, and vague nouns—something like, 'I really think that the way the government handled the crisis was totally terrible and everyone was super upset.' I then ask the students to identify the 'subjective noise.' We systematically strip away the 'I really think' and the 'totally terrible,' replacing them with nominalizations and specific descriptors: 'The government’s crisis management response elicited widespread public dissatisfaction.' This exercise isn't just about grammar; it’s about showing how a shift in register transforms a personal grievance into a debatable scholarly proposition. This is the crucial 'Aha!' moment where learners see that the academic register actually grants their ideas more authority, not less.

Finally, we conclude by discussing the 'Register of Humility' versus the 'Register of Certainty.' One of the most common pitfalls for transitioning writers is the urge to over-claim. I illustrate how using 'suggests,' 'indicates,' or 'may' (hedging) is actually a sign of professional strength in the academy, not a sign of weakness. I guide the students to look at a research report through the lens of expectations: an expert expects a clear roadmap, a neutral tone, and a precise vocabulary. By the end of this session, students should view the academic register as a professional uniform—a necessary set of conventions that allows them to enter the conversation without their persona getting in the way of their contribution.

tasks: Rewrite a colloquial paragraph into a formal academic register suitable for a university professor.
List the typical expectations an expert reader has when approaching a research report.

sessions.title: The Writing Process
sessions.description: This session deconstructs the myth of the 'lone genius' by presenting writing as a recursive, social process. You will learn a multi-stage approach to drafting that reduces anxiety and improves output quality, serving as the roadmap for the rest of this course.
sessions.sessionOutline:
We begin by dismantling the destructive myth of the 'lone genius'—the idea that great academic writing emerges fully formed from a single moment of inspiration. For many students, this myth is the root of writing anxiety and procrastination. On the whiteboard, I draw a single straight line from 'Idea' to 'Finished Paper' and then immediately cross it out with a large 'X'. This linear model is a lie. I replace it with a series of overlapping circles or a spiral, visualizing the writing process as recursive. The goal is to shift the student's mindset from 'performance' (getting it right the first time) to 'process' (layering thoughts over time). This is crucial because it allows them to lower their internal editor's volume during early phases, which is where most 'stuck' moments occur.

To move from the abstract to the concrete, I introduce the concept of 'Writing as a Social Conversation.' I sketch a dinner party scene on the board. You don't just walk in and start shouting; you listen to the current conversation (Research), you form an initial thought (Pre-writing/Brainstorming), you test that thought with a neighbor (Drafting/Feedback), and you refine your statement based on their reaction (Revision). By framing writing as a social act, we emphasize that the 'struggle' is not a sign of failure but a sign of engagement with complex ideas. I explicitly point out that even tenured professors go through multiple messy drafts, positioning the 'shitty first draft' as a necessary, professional milestone rather than a secret shame.

Next, I map out the specific phases of the academic workflow: Discovery, Scaffolding, Drafting, and Refining. I use the whiteboard to show how these phases aren't separate boxes but interconnected gears. I define 'Scaffolding' (outlining and evidence mapping) as the bridge that prevents the common pitfall of 'patchwriting' or getting lost in one's notes. I ask students to look at their own current workflow—do they spend 90% of their time staring at a blank cursor? That is a diagnostic sign of skipping the Discovery and Scaffolding phases. We discuss the 'incubation' period—the time away from the screen—as a legitimate part of the professional process, not as 'wasted time'.

To conclude, we build a hypothetical 10-page paper timeline together on the board. Instead of working forward from a start date, we work backward from a deadline. We allocate 'buffer' zones for the inevitable moments when an argument falls apart or new research is needed. This visualization helps students see that a 10-page paper isn't a 10-hour marathon, but a 3-week project of managed tasks. This session serves as the roadmap for the entire course; by understanding that the process is broken into manageable, recursive steps, students gain the strategic confidence to tackle the high-stakes assignments in Units 2 through 5 without the paralyzing fear of the 'perfect' final product.

tasks: Map out your current writing workflow and identify one area where you typically get 'stuck'.
Create a timeline for a hypothetical 10-page paper including research, drafting, and revision phases.

lectures.title: Reading as a Writer
lectures.description: Develop the ability to deconstruct academic texts not just for content, but for the rhetorical moves authors make to build their authority.

sessions.title: Critical Reading
sessions.description: This session teaches you how to approach a text as a skeptical inquirer rather than a passive recipient. You will gain tools to evaluate evidence and logic, which is the necessary first step before you can contribute your own voice to an academic conversation.
sessions.sessionOutline:
Start this session by challenging the common misconception that academic reading is about 'extracting information' like water from a sponge. On the whiteboard, draw two contrasting icons: a passive receiver and a skeptical inquirer. Explain that in the academy, a text is not a holy scripture of facts but a series of calculated choices made by an author. To read like a writer, students must shift from asking 'What is this saying?' to 'What is the author trying to do to me?' This shift is crucial because it transforms the reader from a consumer into a potential peer who can eventually talk back to the text.

Introduce the concept of the 'Rhetorical Goal.' Draw a triangle representing the Rhetorical Situation (Author, Audience, Subject). Explain that every academic piece is written to solve a problem or fill a gap in a specific conversation. If students can't identify the specific 'problem' the author is solving, they will struggle to evaluate the 'solution' (the argument). Illustrate this by sketching a 'Map of Assumptions'—the invisible foundation of any claim. For example, if an author argues for a new policy, they assume the current policy is failing or that their audience values efficiency over cost. Teach students to look for 'signpost' words like 'therefore,' 'however,' and 'it is essential to note,' which signal the author's underlying logic and priorities.

Transition to the logic of evidence evaluation. Draw a scale on the board. On one side, place 'Claims'; on the other, 'Evidence.' The most common pitfall for beginners is accepting a claim simply because it is printed in a journal. Break this habit by demonstrating how to look for the 'warrant'—the often unstated connection between the data and the conclusion. If a study shows that 80% of students prefer digital textbooks, and the author claims digital textbooks improve learning, the 'warrant' is the assumption that preference equals performance. By visualizing this gap on the board, you show students where the logic can be critiqued without needing to be an expert in the field.

Engage the students in a diagnostic exercise. Present a short, provocative academic passage and ask them to find the 'primary goal' and one 'hidden assumption.' This exercise usually reveals that students focus on the topic (e.g., 'it's about climate change') rather than the rhetorical function (e.g., 'it's trying to redefine the economic impact of carbon taxes'). Correct this by re-centering the discussion on the author's intent. Then, have them draft three critical questions. Guide them away from superficial questions like 'Is this true?' toward architectural questions like 'How would this argument change if we looked at a different demographic?' or 'What alternative explanation does the author ignore?'

Conclude by reinforcing that being a 'skeptical inquirer' isn't about being negative; it's about being rigorous. Explain that by questioning the author’s logic now, they are building the muscles needed to construct their own bulletproof arguments in the upcoming units. The goal of this session is to make the text feel 'built' rather than 'given,' which empowers the student to eventually become a builder themselves.

tasks: Read a short passage and identify the author's primary goal and any underlying assumptions.
Draft three critical questions you would ask the author of a specific study.

sessions.title: Annotation
sessions.description: This session introduces active annotation techniques to help you engage deeply with complex material. You will learn to mark texts for both content and structure, turning reading into a generative act that directly informs your future writing.
sessions.sessionOutline:
In this session, we transition from the general mindset of critical reading to the physical mechanics of scholarly dialogue through annotation. Start by visualizing the text not as a monolith of truth, but as a dense map of a researcher’s labor. Use the whiteboard to contrast 'passive highlighting'—the common student trap of turning a page neon yellow—with 'active coding.' Explain that passive highlighting is merely a record of attention, whereas annotation is a record of thinking. The core concept here is that annotation is the first draft of their future paper; if they mark the text effectively now, they won't have to 're-read' the entire source when they start writing.

Introduce a standardized 'Annotation Legend' on the whiteboard. This should categorize marks into three distinct layers: Structural (what is the text doing?), Substantive (what is the text saying?), and Personal (how am I reacting?). I will demonstrate how to code for 'Claims' (C), 'Evidence' (E), and 'Warrants/Assumptions' (W). The logic here is to decouple the author's voice from the supporting data. A common mistake students make is confusing a cited fact for the author's own argument. By labeling these separately, the student learns to see the 'scaffolding' of academic authority.

Transition to a live demonstration of 'Marginalia as Conversation.' On the whiteboard, simulate a page margin. Show the difference between a summary note like 'Talks about climate change' and a conversational note like 'Challenges Smith (2018) on the basis of methodology.' This second type of note is 'generative' because it creates a bridge between different texts. Explain that these marginal notes serve as 'hooks' for their future synthesis in Unit 4. If they don't talk back to the text now, they will struggle to find their own voice later.

For the practice phase, present a dense paragraph of academic prose. Ask students to apply the legend to identify the primary claim and the specific evidence used to support it. As they do this, watch for 'The Comprehension Barrier'—where a student fails to annotate because they don't understand a specific term. Address this by teaching them to use a '?' symbol for vocabulary or logic gaps, emphasizing that identifying a lack of understanding is itself a sophisticated form of annotation. 

Conclude by having students compare their legends with a peer. This reveals the 'interpretive priority'—one student might have focused entirely on the methodology (E), while another focused on the theoretical implications (C). This comparison is vital because it reinforces the idea that an academic text can be 'used' in multiple ways depending on the reader's research goal. This session transforms the act of reading from a consumer activity into a productive, scholarly labor.

tasks: Annotate a provided page of academic text using a legend that distinguishes between claims, evidence, and your own reactions.
Compare your annotations with a partner's to see different interpretive priorities.

sessions.title: Summarizing Accurately
sessions.description: This session focuses on the skill of neutral, concise summary. You will learn to distill an author's main point without distortion, a foundational skill for building literature reviews and integrating sources effectively later in the course.
sessions.sessionOutline:
Begin the session by framing 'The Summary' not as a clerical task of condensation, but as an intellectual act of compression. On the whiteboard, draw a diamond shape that narrows down to a single point. Explain that in academic discourse, your ability to participate in the 'conversation' (established in Unit 1) is entirely dependent on your ability to represent others' views fairly. If you distort an author's argument, your own subsequent argument becomes a 'straw man' attack, which undermines your credibility or ethos as a scholar. The goal here is to achieve 'The Gist'—the pure, concentrated essence of a text's contribution to knowledge.

Introduce the 'Objective Stance' as the primary technical requirement for academic summary. Use the whiteboard to list 'Evaluative Language' vs. 'Neutral Reporting Verbs.' Illustrate that words like 'claims,' 'argues,' and 'posits' provide a neutral frame, whereas words like 'complains,' 'admits,' or 'brilliantly proves' inject the writer's bias. A common pitfall for learners is the 'Opinion Leak,' where they accidentally praise or criticize the text within the summary. Teach the 'Reverse Engineering' method: looking at a text and identifying the core thesis statement, then stripping away all supporting examples, anecdotes, and data until only the skeletal argument remains. This demonstrates that a summary is a map of the forest, not a description of every tree.

Transition to a practical diagnostic exercise. Present a short, emotionally charged or intellectually dense academic summary that includes subtle evaluative adjectives (e.g., 'The author makes an *aggressive* argument' or 'This *persuasive* study shows'). Ask learners to act as 'Neutrality Editors' to strike out the subjective modifiers. The pedagogical intent here is to reveal how deeply our personal judgment is embedded in our vocabulary. By stripping these words away, students learn that a summary's power comes from its accuracy and brevity, not its adjective count. Explain that in a literature review, if the reader can tell whether you like the author or not based on your summary, you have failed the neutrality test.

Conclude by introducing the 'One-Sentence Gist' challenge. On the board, write the formula: '[Author Name] [Neutral Verb] [Core Argument/Contribution] in order to [Purpose].' This structure prevents the common mistake of 'The List' summary, where students simply list what happened in each paragraph ('First he says this, then he says that'). Instead, it forces them to grasp the holistic intent of the piece. Finish the session by emphasizing that mastering the neutral summary is the 'gatekeeper skill' for Unit 4’s synthesis; you cannot weave multiple voices together if you cannot first capture each voice individually and accurately.

tasks: Write a one-sentence summary (the 'gist') of a complex academic article.
Identify and remove 'evaluative' language from a biased summary to make it neutral.

sessions.title: Responding to a Text
sessions.description: This session bridges the gap between summary and analysis. You will learn how to formulate a scholarly response that adds value rather than just repeating information, preparing you to enter the conversation as an independent thinker.
sessions.sessionOutline:
In this final session of Unit 1, we move from being observers of academic writing to participants. I start by visualizing the 'Academic Conversation' on the whiteboard: imagine a dinner party where guests have been discussing a topic for hours before you arrived. You cannot just walk in and shout your opinion; you must first listen, then acknowledge what was said, and finally add your unique contribution. This session is designed to break the habit of 'refrigerator journalism'—the tendency of novice writers to simply list what others have said without adding their own intellectual value.

I introduce the concept of 'Responding' through the rhetorical framework of templates. The whiteboard should display three clear paths: 'Yes, and...', 'No, because...', and 'Yes, but...'. The most important idea here is that a scholarly response must do more than just agree or disagree; it must provide a reason that moves the conversation forward. For example, agreeing is only valuable if you provide a new application or additional evidence that the original author missed. Disagreeing is only scholarly if it points to a flaw in logic, data, or a shift in context. This framing helps students realize that their voice gains authority not by being loud, but by being logically situated in relation to others.

To help students master these moves, we will practice with a 'Yes, but...' scenario. I present a common academic claim—for instance, 'Digital learning improves student outcomes by providing 24/7 access to materials.' I then ask students to brainstorm the 'but.' Does it overlook the digital divide? Does it ignore the importance of face-to-face mentorship? The goal of this exercise is to reveal that 'reading as a writer' means looking for the gaps or the 'unsaid' in a text. We want to avoid the common pitfall where students feel they aren't 'expert enough' to disagree. I address this by explaining that their specific context—as a student in a particular field or a member of a specific demographic—is exactly the source of their unique scholarly authority.

Finally, we transition to connecting these responses to the student's own research interests. On the board, I draw a bridge from a specific source (the summary they created in the previous session) to their potential research paper. I ask them to draft a 'contribution statement.' This isn't a full argument yet, but a declaration of how they intend to use the source: as a foundation to build upon, a counterpoint to challenge, or a lens through which to view their own data. This practice ensures that they aren't just 'collecting' sources for their course project, but are actively 'employing' them to carve out their own intellectual space.

tasks: Use the 'Yes, and...', 'No, because...', or 'Yes, but...' templates to respond to a specific academic claim.
Outline a brief response to an article that connects it to your own research interests.

lectures.title: Getting Started
lectures.description: Move from a general area of interest to a concrete, viable research plan that sets the stage for a successful academic paper.

sessions.title: From Topic to Research Question
sessions.description: This session teaches you how to narrow a broad topic into a specific, answerable research question. You will learn the criteria for a 'good' question, which prevents the common pitfall of starting a project that is too vast or too simple to be academic.
sessions.sessionOutline:
Begin the session by addressing the 'Iceberg Problem' in academic writing: most novices try to write about the entire visible iceberg (a broad topic), whereas scholars focus on a single, jagged edge beneath the surface. Using the whiteboard, draw a large circle representing a broad interest area like 'Artificial Intelligence.' Explain that while this topic is exciting, it is commercially and intellectually unmanageable for a single paper. The goal today is to move from interest to an 'intervention.' We do this not by discarding ideas, but by applying successive filters—Time, Place, and Perspective—to transform a noun into a question.

Demonstrate the narrowing process through a live visualization. Start with 'Climate Change.' Draw an arrow to a narrower sub-topic: 'Climate Change Policy.' Then, apply a specific lens, such as 'Urban Planning in Coastal Cities.' Finally, reach the level of a research question: 'How have zoning laws in Miami influenced local adaptation to rising sea levels since 2010?' Highlight that the final question is specific enough to suggest a methodology and a clear boundary for research. This progression illustrates that a good research question is a compass, not a destination; it tells you where to look and, more importantly, what you can safely ignore.

Introduce the 'So What?' test as the primary filter for academic rigor. A common pitfall for students is crafting a question that is 'answerable' but 'insignificant' (e.g., 'How many people use TikTok?'). On the whiteboard, contrast this with an academic question: 'How does TikTok's algorithmic feed impact the attention span of secondary school students during homework?' The 'So What?' test requires the writer to justify the inquiry by connecting it to a larger debate or a practical problem. If the answer to the question doesn't change how we think about a subject or solve a problem, it’s a 'dead-end question.'

Transition to an interactive evaluation of sample questions. Present three variations: one that is too broad ('Is social media bad?'), one that is a simple fact-check ('What year was the first social media site launched?'), and one that is a viable research question ('How does the use of Instagram's photo-editing filters correlate with body dysmorphia among adolescent girls?'). Ask the students to rank these based on the feasibility of finding evidence and the depth of the resulting argument. This helps them recognize that a viable question must be 'open'—meaning there isn't a single consensus answer—and 'complex'—requiring a synthesis of various data points rather than a simple Google search.

Conclude by reinforcing the idea that research questions are iterative. Warn students against the 'Commitment Trap'—the fear that once a question is written, it cannot change. In reality, as they discover sources in the next units, the question will likely shrink or shift. Use the final whiteboard space to map out the relationship between the question and the upcoming project proposal: the question is the seed, the proposal is the soil. If the seed is too large, it won't take root; if it's too small, it won't grow into a full-length paper.

tasks: Take a broad topic (e.g., 'Climate Change') and narrow it down through three levels of specificity.
Evaluate three sample research questions using the 'So What?' test.

sessions.title: Freewriting and Brainstorming
sessions.description: This session introduces low-stakes writing techniques to overcome 'blank page' syndrome. You will learn how to use generative writing to discover what you actually think, turning vague ideas into concrete concepts that can be organized later.
sessions.sessionOutline:
In this public-lecture style session, we address the psychological and cognitive 'bottleneck' of academic writing: the fear of the blank page and the paralyzing 'internal editor.' We begin by visualizing the mind not as a structured filing cabinet, but as a messy workshop. The core concept here is 'generative writing'—the idea that we do not write to record thoughts we have already mastered, but rather we write to discover what those thoughts are in the first place. This shifts the focus from 'correctness' to 'exploration,' which is essential for developing original scholarly contributions.

I will start the whiteboard by drawing a divide between the 'Creator' and the 'Critic.' Most students struggle because they invite the Critic—the part of the brain focused on grammar, citations, and logic—to the table too early. We will define 'Freewriting' as a deliberate act of silencing the Critic. The key instruction here is kinetic: the pen must never stop moving. If you run out of ideas, you write 'I don't know what to say' until a new thought emerges. This physical continuity bypasses the cognitive 'stutter' of self-doubt. It’s important to emphasize that the output of this session isn't meant to be 'good'; it’s meant to be 'material.'

Transitioning into the 'Focused Freewrite' practice, I will ask learners to take the research question they developed in the previous session and treat it as a prompt. The logic here is that by writing continuously for ten minutes, the brain eventually tires of superficial answers and begins to tap into deeper associations. A common pitfall is that students will try to write 'academic-sounding' sentences during this phase. I will explicitly instruct them to use their natural voice, even slang or shorthand, to ensure the flow of ideas is not throttled by the search for the 'perfect' academic register.

Once the page is full of messy, unorganized text, we move to the 'Clustering' or 'Concept Mapping' phase on the whiteboard. This represents the first stage of organization where we start to see the 'skeleton' of the argument. I will demonstrate how to circle key nouns or recurring themes in their freewriting and draw lines to connect them. This visualizes the cognitive relationship between disparate ideas. For example, if a student is writing about 'Urban Design,' they might find they’ve mentioned 'mental health,' 'green spaces,' and 'socio-economic status.' Mapping these reveals that their argument isn't just about 'parks,' but about 'the impact of green infrastructure on the mental well-being of low-income populations.'

Finally, we conclude by evaluating the map to identify 'islands'—ideas that have no connections—and 'hubs'—ideas that everything else seems to point toward. This diagnostic moment is crucial because it tells the student where their true interest lies and where they need more evidence. We end the session by emphasizing that these scribbles are the DNA of their future paper, transforming the overwhelming task of 'writing an essay' into the manageable task of 'connecting the dots' they have already created.

tasks: Complete a 10-minute focused freewriting exercise on your chosen research question.
Create a concept map (clustering) to visualize the relationships between your brainstormed ideas.

sessions.title: Outlining
sessions.description: This session explains how to create a structural blueprint for your paper. You will learn to use outlines to test the logic of your argument before you invest time in drafting, ensuring a clear path for your reader to follow.
sessions.sessionOutline:
In this session, we transition from the chaotic creativity of brainstorming to the architectural rigor of outlining. I begin by positioning the outline not as a formal requirement to be checked off, but as a 'stress test' for logic. I want to emphasize that it is far easier to fix a structural collapse in a bulleted list than in a ten-page draft. On the whiteboard, I draw a skeletal structure alongside a finished building; the goal is to show that while the building is what people see, the skeleton determines if it stands. We must shift the learner's mindset from 'what I want to say' to 'how I will prove it step-by-step.'

I then introduce the concept of 'Hierarchical Logic.' Instead of just listing topics, an academic outline must demonstrate subordination and coordination. I'll use a whiteboard diagram to show how a 'Level 1' heading represents a major claim, while 'Level 2' sub-points represent the evidence or warrants supporting that claim. A common pitfall for students is 'lopsided outlining,' where one section is overly detailed and another is empty. I will explain that a thin section in an outline is a red flag—it means you either don't have enough evidence or your argument has hit a dead end before it even began. By visualizing these levels, students learn to spot intellectual gaps early.

The core of the lecture focuses on the 'Thematic Thread.' I will demonstrate how to check if every sub-point actually 'talks back' to the central research question. To do this, I'll present a flawed outline on the board where one point is technically interesting but rhetorically irrelevant. I’ll ask students to find the 'imposter.' This exercise is crucial because it teaches them the discipline of exclusion—academic writing is as much about what you leave out as what you put in. We will discuss the 'Missing Link' phenomenon, where a writer jumps from Point A to Point C without providing the logical bridge (Point B) that the reader needs to follow the journey.

Finally, we move into the transition from ideas to draft-readiness. I will show how to turn a keyword-only outline into a 'Sentence Outline.' By forcing ourselves to write full thematic sentences for each major heading, we ensure that each paragraph has a clear topic sentence. This prevents the 'data dump' where a student just lists facts without an argumentative claim. I conclude by having the students take their chaotic notes from the previous session and organize them into this hierarchical format, looking specifically for places where their logic leaps too far or where their evidence is too thin to support the weight of their claim.

tasks: Convert a list of brainstormed points into a logical hierarchical outline.
Identify the 'missing links' in a provided flawed outline.

sessions.title: Planning a Draft
sessions.description: This session covers the logistics of the first draft, including goal setting and resource management. You will create a concrete plan for your course project, ensuring you have a clear strategy for the upcoming units on argumentation and structure.
sessions.sessionOutline:
In this final session of Unit 1, we move from the abstract conceptualization of ideas to the logistical reality of project management. The primary goal is to strip away the intimidation of the 'Final Paper' by treating it as a series of manageable, strategic logistics. I begin by defining the Project Proposal not as a rigid contract, but as a 'mission statement.' On the whiteboard, I draw a simple compass: the needle represents the research question, and the cardinal directions represent the initial plan for inquiry. The central concept here is that a draft is not a performance of knowledge, but a roadmap for discovery; by articulating a 200-word proposal now, students commit to a trajectory that prevents the 'wandering scholar' syndrome where research lacks a focal point.

I transition into the 'Source Infrastructure' phase. Most students wait until they are writing to look for sources, which leads to 'patchwriting'—fitting sources into a pre-existing argument regardless of fit. To counteract this, I visualize a 'Resource Ecosystem' on the board. We categorize sources not just as 'books' or 'articles,' but by their functional utility: foundational theory, empirical evidence, or counter-argument. I explain that identifying these needs early acts as a diagnostic for the research question itself; if you can't imagine what kind of data would answer your question, the question is likely too vague or too philosophical for this level of academic writing.

Next, we address the 'Project Timeline' and potential bottlenecks. I introduce the 'Buffer Zone' concept—planning for the reality that certain sources will be unavailable or that an initial hypothesis might be proven wrong. I encourage students to list not just what they know they need, but the 'Missing Pieces'—the specific gaps in their current knowledge that require external validation. This shifts the mindset from 'collecting facts' to 'targeted problem solving.' I explicitly warn against the 'Encyclopedia Trap,' where students plan to gather every piece of information on a topic rather than focusing only on what is necessary to sustain their specific argument.

To conclude, we move into the actual construction of the 200-word proposal. I provide a template on the board: 'Problem -> Question -> Proposed Method -> Expected Significance.' The 'So What?' test returns here as the final filter. As students begin drafting their proposals and source lists, I circulate to ensure their plans are 'viable'—meaning they have access to the necessary types of evidence and a question narrow enough to be answered within the course's constraints. This session unlocks the upcoming units on argumentation and structure by ensuring every student has a concrete, logical anchor to which they can apply new skills.

tasks: Write a 200-word project proposal summarizing your research question and initial plan.
List the types of sources you anticipate needing to answer your question.

projects.stage_description: Define a narrow research topic and transform it into a viable research question. Create a 300-word proposal that outlines your intended audience and the significance of the inquiry.
projects.deliverable_increment: A formal Research Proposal and Outlining Document.

exams.title: The Academic Writing Situation Assessment
exams.goal: Evaluate the student's ability to analyze rhetorical situations, perform critical readings, and formulate a viable academic research plan.
sections: This comprehensive exam covers the transition to academic writing, the application of critical reading and annotation strategies, and the technical process of moving from a broad interest to a structured research question and project plan.
successCriteria: Correctly identify features of academic register vs. informal writing.
Demonstrate the ability to summarize a scholarly text without bias.
Refine a broad topic into a narrow, arguable research question.
Identify the generic conventions of different academic disciplines.

units.title: Building an Argument
units.description: This unit focuses on the intellectual core of academic prose: the argument. Using the Toulmin model of argumentation, students learn to move from simple opinions to complex, evidence-supported claims while anticipating and addressing scholarly objections.

lectures.title: Thesis and Claim
lectures.description: In this lecture, we move from the initial research question developed in Unit 1 to the creation of a formal, arguable thesis statement and the breakdown of that thesis into constituent claims and warrants.

sessions.title: What a Thesis Does
sessions.description: This session explores the rhetorical function of a thesis statement as the 'contract' between the writer and the reader. You will learn to identify the difference between a topic, a question, and a formal thesis, allowing you to establish a clear direction for your academic work. Mastering this function is essential for moving beyond descriptive writing and meeting the expectations of a scholarly audience.
sessions.sessionOutline:
In this opening session, we transition the student from the 'informational' mindset of high school writing to the 'argumentative' mindset of the academy. Begin by sketching a triangle on the whiteboard representing the rhetorical situation: Writer, Audience, and Subject. Explain that in most novice writing, the 'Subject' is the only thing the student focuses on—essentially acting as a human encyclopedia. Contrast this with the 'Thesis,' which I define not as a topic, but as a 'contract.' On the board, draw a line between the Writer and the Audience; label this line the 'Thesis Contract.' This visual establishes that a thesis is a promise to the reader that the writer will prove a specific point, creating a mutual expectation that dictates everything from word choice to evidence selection.

To help students internalize this concept, visualize the progression from 'Topic' to 'Question' to 'Thesis' as a narrowing funnel. Start with a broad circle labeled 'Climate Change' (the Topic). Then, draw an arrow to a question mark labeled 'How does urban heat impact local economies?' (the Question). Finally, draw a sharp, directed arrow to a solid block labeled 'Urban heat islands are the primary drivers of municipal budget deficits due to infrastructure cooling costs' (the Thesis). Explain that while many students stop at the question stage, the academic reader requires the 'answer'—the thesis—to be stated upfront so they know exactly what they are evaluating. This prevents the common misconception that a thesis should be a 'surprise' saved for the end of the paper.

Now, introduce a diagnostic moment to distinguish between 'Truth' and 'Thesis.' Present three short texts on the board: a purely descriptive passage (e.g., 'The sun rises in the east'), a statement of personal taste (e.g., 'Sunny days are better than rainy days'), and a formal thesis (e.g., 'The psychological association between sunlight and productivity justifies flexible working hours in northern latitudes'). Guide the learners to see that the first is unarguable because it's a fact, the second is unarguable because it's a private preference, and only the third invites a scholarly conversation because it requires evidence and logic to sustain. This 'conversation' metaphor is key: a thesis is an invitation to a debate, not a lecture on a fixed reality.

Conclude the session by having the students practice the 'Purpose Statement' bridge. Explain that before a full thesis can be polished, a writer needs a 'north star.' On the whiteboard, provide a template: 'In this paper, I am arguing [X] because [Y].' Ask the students to apply this to a sample topic like 'Digital Privacy.' The goal here isn't a perfect sentence, but a functional one that moves them from 'I am writing about privacy' to 'I am arguing that privacy is a commodity because it can be traded for convenience.' This exercise reveals whether the student has actually identified an intervention they want to make in the subject matter or if they are still just describing it. Stress that this purpose statement is the internal engine of their draft, ensuring their work has a clear, singular direction from the first paragraph.

tasks: Compare three short texts and identify which one contains a true thesis vs. a simple statement of fact.
Draft a one-sentence 'purpose statement' for a sample research topic.

sessions.title: Writing an Arguable Thesis
sessions.description: This session focuses on the 'arguable' quality of a thesis, distinguishing it from settled facts or purely personal preferences. You will learn the 'So What?' test to ensure your thesis addresses a meaningful problem within your field of study. This skill is critical for ensuring your project has sufficient depth to sustain a full-length academic paper.
sessions.sessionOutline:
Start the session by drawing a sharp line down the center of the whiteboard. On one side, write 'Settled Facts'; on the other, write 'Dynamic Debates.' Explain that many students mistakenly believe a thesis is a summary of reality—a safe statement that everyone agrees with to avoid being 'wrong.' We must immediately dismantle this safety-first approach. A thesis that everyone agrees with is not an academic contribution; it is an encyclopedia entry. Use a simple example: 'The Earth orbits the sun' is a fact, but 'The colonization of Mars is a moral necessity for human survival' is a thesis. The difference lies in the potential for a reasonable person to disagree. If no one can say 'I disagree' to your statement, you don't have a thesis; you have a premise.

Introduce the 'So What?' Test as the primary diagnostic tool for evaluating intellectual weight. Write 'So What?' in large letters on the board. Explain that this question represents the skeptical reader who is asking why this research matters to the field. A thesis might be arguable but trivial, such as 'Blue is a better color for school uniforms than red.' While debatable, it lacks the 'So What?' factor—it doesn't solve a problem or challenge a significant assumption in a discipline. Transition into the 'Problem-Solution' framework: a strong thesis identifies a tension, a contradiction, or a gap in understanding and offers a specific, debatable interpretation to resolve it. This prevents the student from falling into the trap of 'personal preference' writing, where opinions are shared without scholarly stakes.

Now, conduct a live diagnostic using the five provided sample statements. Present a 'Factual' statement like 'Digital social media has changed how people communicate' and ask the class why this fails. Most will see it's true, but show them it's too broad and non-debatable. Then, contrast it with an 'Arguable' version: 'Social media algorithms have eroded the democratic process by prioritizing engagement over truth.' The goal here is to show how adding a specific stance and a cause-effect relationship creates a 'burden of proof' for the writer. This 'burden' is actually a good thing; it gives the writer a specific job to do in the subsequent paragraphs.

Address the common misconception that being 'debatable' means being 'extreme' or 'provocative' for the sake of it. Clarify that academic arguability is grounded in evidence and logic, not volume. Use the whiteboard to map out a 'Revision Flow': start with a weak, descriptive claim, identify its 'missing stake' (the So What?), and then add a qualifying 'although' or 'because' clause to give it complexity. For the final practice, have students take a flat, non-arguable claim—such as 'Recycling is good for the environment'—and force them to revise it into something that could be debated at a policy or scientific level. This exercise reveals whether they understand that a thesis is a tool for professional intervention, not just a label for a topic.

tasks: Apply the 'So What?' test to five provided thesis statements and label them as 'Arguable' or 'Factual'.
Revise a weak, non-arguable claim into a strong, debatable thesis.

sessions.title: Claims and Reasons
sessions.description: In this session, we break down the main thesis into smaller, manageable sub-claims supported by logical reasons. You will learn to use 'Because' clauses to link your claims to supporting logic, creating a roadmap for your body paragraphs. This provides the logical architecture necessary for a systematic mastery of academic persuasion.
sessions.sessionOutline:
Start the session by visualizing the thesis statement not as a static sentence, but as the 'engine' of the entire essay. On the whiteboard, draw the thesis as a central hub with several branching lines leading outward. Explain that while the thesis tells us *what* the writer believes, it doesn't explain *why* the reader should care or agree. This is where we introduce the concept of the 'sub-claim' as the logical bridge between the main argument and the specific evidence. The most important takeaway here is that a sub-claim is never just a fact; it is a miniature argument in its own right that supports the larger whole.

Introduce the 'Thesis because Reason' formula as the primary tool for structural architecture. Write a sample thesis on the board, such as 'Urban vertical farming is the most viable solution for future food security.' Then, demonstrate how to add 'because' clauses. Explain that the word 'because' acts as a logical hinge, forcing the writer to articulate a reason rather than just listing topics. For example, '...because it minimizes transportation emissions,' or '...because it allows for year-round production regardless of climate.' Show how these 'reasons' immediately become the topic sentences for the body paragraphs, creating a pre-built roadmap for the reader.

A common pitfall for students is creating sub-claims that are either too broad (re-stating the thesis) or too narrow (stating a data point). To prevent this, lead a whiteboard exercise where you deconstruct a complex academic thesis into three distinct pillars. Use the 'Umbrella Test': if a sub-claim doesn't fit under the 'umbrella' of the main thesis, it belongs in a different paper; if the sub-claim is the same size as the umbrella, it isn't specific enough to be a sub-claim. This visualization helps learners understand the hierarchical nature of academic logic.

Transition into the practice phase by having students look at their own project topics. Instead of letting them dive into writing, have them map out their 'Reason' branches on a sketchpad or digital whiteboard. The goal of the 'Thesis because Reason' formula practice is to reveal logical gaps early. If a student struggles to find three distinct 'becausals,' it usually indicates that their thesis is either a statement of fact (which has no reasons) or is too shallow for a full research project. Use this moment to pivot toward refinement, showing how a lack of sub-claims is actually a diagnostic tool for a weak central argument.

Conclude by emphasizing that this session represents the shift from 'what I think' to 'how I will prove it.' By the end of the whiteboard session, the board should look like a skeletal map of an essay. Explain that a well-structured set of claims and reasons allows the writer to maintain control over the narrative, ensuring that every paragraph serves a specific rhetorical purpose in advancing the main thesis. This 'logical architecture' is what separates a professional scholarly argument from a simple collection of observations.

tasks: Deconstruct a sample thesis into three distinct sub-claims.
Write three sub-claims for your own project thesis using the 'Thesis because Reason' formula.

sessions.title: Warrants and Assumptions
sessions.description: This session introduces the 'warrant'—the underlying assumption that connects a claim to its support. You will learn to identify and evaluate these unstated bridges to ensure your argument is logically sound and persuasive to a skeptical reader. Understanding warrants is a hallmark of advanced academic writing and prevents logical gaps in your reasoning.
sessions.sessionOutline:
We begin this session by addressing the 'silent' element of the Toulmin model: the warrant. I want to frame this not as a technical jargon, but as the invisible glue that makes an argument stick. In public lecture style, I’ll start with a provocative, everyday example—something like 'It's raining, so you should take an umbrella.' On the whiteboard, I’ll draw the 'Claim' (take an umbrella) and the 'Reason' (it's raining). Then, I’ll draw a bridge between them and ask: 'What are we assuming to be true for this to work?' This reveals the warrant: 'Umbrellas keep you dry' or 'It is undesirable to get wet.' This first step is crucial because it moves the learner from seeing arguments as two-part structures (A because of B) to three-part structures (A because of B, provided that C is true).

Moving into the academic context, I will explain that a warrant is a shared value or logical principle that the writer and reader must agree upon for the evidence to successfully support the claim. This is where many students fail; they assume their reader shares their worldview. I will visualize this on the board as a 'Logical Gap.' If the writer provides evidence that 'Online classes allow for flexible scheduling' to support the claim 'Online classes are superior to in-person classes,' the unstated warrant is 'Flexible scheduling is the primary metric of educational quality.' By making this visible, I can show learners how a skeptical reader—perhaps a professor who values face-to-face mentorship—would immediately reject the argument because they do not accept the warrant. This shift in perspective is the hallmark of advanced academic writing: anticipating the reader’s internal logic.

To deepen this conceptual understanding, we will engage in a 'Syllogism Stress Test.' I’ll present three syllogisms on the board and ask the students to extract the hidden premise. For example, 'The author uses five different metaphors, so the writing is high quality.' The warrant here is 'The density of metaphorical language is a sign of literary merit.' I will challenge the students to imagine a reader who wouldn't buy that—perhaps a scientist who values clarity and literalism over metaphor. This exercise is designed to reveal the subjectivity inherent in scholarly debate and teaches students that they must either choose warrants their audience already accepts or explicitly 'back' their warrants with further argument.

Finally, we will address the risk of 'Warrant Blindness'—the tendency to believe our logic is universal. I will walk through a sample argument where the warrant is culturally or disciplinarily specific, such as an argument about economic efficiency that assumes 'Profit maximization is always the goal.' I’ll prompt the students to evaluate this: what happens if the audience is a non-profit or a social enterprise? By the end of this session, students should not just be identifying warrants, but evaluating the 'persuasive fit' between their logic and their intended scholarly audience, ensuring no logical bridges are left unbuilt or undefended.

tasks: Identify the unstated warrant in three provided syllogisms.
Evaluate a sample argument and explain why a specific audience might reject its warrant.

lectures.title: Evidence
lectures.description: This lecture transitions from the logical structure of claims to the empirical or textual support required to prove them, focusing on the selection, interpretation, and analysis of evidence.

sessions.title: Types of Evidence
sessions.description: This session categorizes the various forms of evidence used across disciplines, from quantitative data to qualitative anecdotes and textual citations. You will learn which types of evidence are most persuasive for different scholarly audiences, helping you select the right tools for your specific research question. This provides the foundational knowledge needed to build credible, evidence-based arguments.
sessions.sessionOutline:
Welcome students to the engine room of argumentation: Evidence. In this concept-first public lecture, we begin by shifting the mindset away from 'having an opinion' toward 'building a case.' I will start by drawing a central axis on the whiteboard representing the spectrum of academic disciplines. On one end, place the 'Hard Sciences/Quantitative' and on the other, 'Humanities/Qualitative.' The core concept here is that evidence is not a universal currency; its value is dictated by the scholarly community you are addressing. Explain that while a chemist seeks reproducibility and statistical significance, a literary scholar seeks depth of insight and textual nuance. This sets the stage for understanding that 'good' evidence is context-dependent.

Now, let's populate this spectrum with specific types. I will draw three distinct buckets on the board: Empirical Data (statistics, experimental results), Textual/Expert Testimony (quotes, archival documents, peer-reviewed theory), and Anecdotal/Case Study evidence. As I draw these, I'll emphasize the 'Hierarchy of Persuasion.' For instance, in a public policy paper, a single moving anecdote about a family might open the introduction to hook the reader, but the 'work' of the argument must be done by the statistical data in the middle. I'll warn students about the 'Anecdotal Fallacy'—the mistake of assuming a single story proves a universal rule—and explain that in academia, we use anecdotes to illustrate, not to prove.

To bridge the gap between abstract types and real-world application, we will engage in a matching exercise. I'll list disciplines like 'Sociology,' 'Mechanical Engineering,' and 'History' on one side, and ask the class to assign the most 'potent' evidence type to each. This isn't just about labeling; it's about uncovering the 'Warrant' (the logic connecting evidence to claim). For example, why is a case study highly valued in Clinical Psychology but viewed as 'low-level' in Macroeconomics? This reveals the underlying epistemological differences in how different fields define 'truth.'

We will then move to a 'Dual-Evidence Brainstorm.' I will write a provocative claim on the board, such as: 'The shift to remote work has permanently altered urban economies.' Instead of looking for one perfect piece of evidence, I’ll challenge the class to find two radically different types—perhaps a set of GDP statistics from a central bank and a series of qualitative interviews with small business owners. This exercise is designed to show that 'triangulation'—using multiple types of evidence—creates a much more resilient argument. It prevents the 'single-source' weakness where an opponent can dismiss your entire paper by debunking one specific data point.

Finally, I will address the common misconception that more evidence is always better. I will draw a 'Diminishing Returns' curve on the board. One piece of evidence is a suggestion; two or three well-chosen pieces from different angles are a proof; ten pieces of the same type are often just noise. The goal for a scholarly writer is 'Representative Sufficiency'—providing enough variety and depth that the reader feels it would be unreasonable to disagree, without burying the actual logic of the argument under a mountain of raw data.

tasks: Match types of evidence (statistics, case studies, expert testimony) to specific academic disciplines.
Brainstorm two different types of evidence that could support a single claim.

sessions.title: Selecting Evidence
sessions.description: This session teaches you how to curate evidence based on relevance, sufficiency, and representative quality. You will learn to distinguish between 'cherry-picked' data and a robust evidence base, ensuring your argument stands up to peer scrutiny. This skill is vital for maintaining academic integrity and constructing a professional-level defense of your claims.
sessions.sessionOutline:
In this public lecture-style session, we transition from identifying 'what' evidence is to the more critical skill of 'curating' it. Begin by visualizing a courtroom or a scientific review board: the goal isn't to present every piece of information available, but to present the most compelling, undeniable proof. Introduce the 'STAR' criteria (Sufficiency, Typicality, Accuracy, and Relevance) as the primary filter. We focus on the concept that a mountain of weak evidence is far less persuasive than three pillars of high-quality data. On the whiteboard, draw a funnel—at the top, the chaotic mass of raw data; at the bottom, the refined 'robust evidence base' that serves the specific claim.

The first core concept is Relevance. I will demonstrate that 'interesting' is not the same as 'relevant.' Using a hypothetical claim about the economic impact of urban green spaces, I'll show how a beautiful poem about a park (textual evidence) fails the relevance test compared to a property value study (quantitative evidence) for this specific argument. The logic here is that relevance is defined by the 'warrant'—the bridge we discussed in the Toulmin model. If the evidence doesn't feed directly into the logic of the claim, it creates 'noise' that distracts the reader. We must guard against the common student mistake of 'citation padding,' where they include sources just to meet a count rather than to strengthen the logic.

Next, we address the danger of 'cherry-picking.' This is where I'll introduce the concept of 'Representative Quality' or Typicality. I want students to imagine a scientist who only reports the three successful trials out of a hundred. On the whiteboard, I’ll diagram a 'skewed sample' vs. a 'representative sample.' The most important takeaway here is that for an argument to be academically honest and professionally robust, it must account for the broader reality of the subject matter. To practice this, we will look at a list of ten sources and identify which ones represent the 'consensus' versus the 'outliers,' teaching students that while outliers are interesting, building a primary claim on them is intellectually risky.

We conclude with the 'Weak Link' diagnostic. Every argument is only as strong as its most questionable piece of support. I will present a sample evidence set for a claim and intentionally include one piece of evidence that is outdated or biased. The goal is to train students to be their own harshest critics. By identifying the 'weak link' in a set, they learn that academic writing is an exercise in quality control. We will practice justifying the exclusion of sources, helping them understand that in professional scholarly output, the decision to leave something out is often as important as the decision to put it in.

tasks: From a list of ten sources, select the three most relevant to a provided claim and justify your choice.
Identify a potential 'weak link' in a sample evidence set.

sessions.title: Interpreting Evidence
sessions.description: In this session, we focus on the 'bridge' between data and conclusion: interpretation. You will learn that evidence does not speak for itself and that the writer must explain how the data supports the claim. This moves your writing from a simple report to a sophisticated analysis, a key requirement for university-level prose.
sessions.sessionOutline:
We begin this session by challenging the common student misconception that evidence is self-explanatory. In a concept-first public lecture style, I will draw a 'gap' on the whiteboard between a pile of raw data (the evidence) and the final conclusion (the claim). I will explain that many writers treat their evidence like a 'mic drop'—expecting the reader to see exactly what they see—but in academic discourse, the writer is the architect of the connection. The central idea is that evidence provides the 'what,' while interpretation provides the 'so what.' Without this bridge, we are merely reporting facts rather than constructing an argument.

To visualize this, I will draw a three-part structural diagram: the Evidence (the anchor), the Interpretation (the bridge), and the Claim (the destination). I'll use a simple, non-academic analogy first—like a detective showing a fingerprint (evidence) to prove a suspect was in the room (claim). The interpretation is the logic explaining that a fingerprint cannot exist without physical contact. I will emphasize that in scholarship, this 'logic of contact' is often complex and requires explicit articulation. The goal here is to shift the learner's mindset from 'sharing information' to 'shaping perception.'

Next, we move to the 'Three-Sentence Rule' for interpretation. I will demonstrate on the board how to move from a data point to a meaningful insight. Sentence one identifies the specific detail; sentence two explains the mechanism or logic (how this detail works); and sentence three ties it back to the overarching claim. I will warn against the 'data dump' where students list three or four statistics in a row without a single sentence of analysis. I’ll provide a sample chart showing a decline in voter turnout and demonstrate two different interpretations: one focusing on 'voter apathy' and another on 'systemic barriers.' This shows the learner that the same evidence can serve different masters depending on the writer's interpretative lens.

We will then transition to a diagnostic exercise where students analyze a pre-written paragraph. I will ask them to physically circle the evidence and underline the interpretation. This usually reveals a common 'weak link': paragraphs that are 90% evidence and 10% interpretation. I will explain that a balanced scholarly paragraph often maintains a 1:2 ratio of evidence to interpretation. This is where we address the 'intuition' tag—teaching students to feel the 'weight' of their own prose and recognize when they are leaving the reader to do too much intellectual heavy lifting.

Finally, I will introduce the concept of 'Warrants' from the Toulmin model discussed in Unit 2, showing how interpretation is essentially the act of making a warrant visible. We will conclude by looking at a piece of professional prose where the 'raw data' is minimal but the 'analytical bridge' is robust. This prepares them for the next session on Analysis vs. Description by proving that the value of an academic paper lies not in the quantity of facts it contains, but in the quality of the connections it makes between those facts and the world of ideas.

tasks: Write a 3-sentence interpretation of a provided data chart that connects it to a specific claim.
Analyze a paragraph and highlight the sentences that serve as 'interpretation' vs. 'raw evidence'.

sessions.title: Analysis vs Description
sessions.description: This session addresses one of the most common pitfalls in student writing: over-describing rather than analyzing. You will learn to use analytical verbs and structural techniques to transform a summary into a critical evaluation. Mastering this distinction is the primary goal for students seeking professional mastery of academic discourse.
sessions.sessionOutline:
The distinction between analysis and description is often the 'glass ceiling' that prevents students from moving into upper-tier academic success. I will begin by framing the whiteboard with a dichotomy: the 'Reporter' vs. the 'Critic.' The Reporter asks 'What?' while the Critic asks 'So What?' and 'How?'. This visualization helps students realize that while description tells us what is happening in a text or data set, analysis interrogates the mechanism and meaning. I need to emphasize that description is the 'floor'—it provides the necessary context—but analysis is the 'ceiling,' where the actual intellectual work occurs.

To move beyond the basic 'what,' I will introduce the concept of 'Analytical Verbs.' On the whiteboard, I'll draw a list of 'Dead Verbs' (says, shows, is, describes) next to 'Strong Verbs' (interrogates, destabilizes, validates, complicates). The core idea here is that the verb is the engine of the sentence; if the verb is passive or merely descriptive, the entire thought remains stagnant. I will demonstrate this by taking a bland sentence like 'The author describes the economic crisis' and transforming it into 'The author interrogates the underlying systemic failures that precipitated the economic crisis.' This shift shows that analysis isn't just about adding more words; it's about using more precise, active conceptual tools.

I will then address a common misconception: that analysis means 'sharing an opinion.' This is where students often veer into subjective territory. I must clarify that academic analysis is 'evidence-based evaluation.' It is not about whether you liked the text, but about how the text functions within a specific framework. I’ll use a diagram of a bridge to illustrate this: on one side is the Raw Data (the evidence), and on the other is the Scholarly Argument (the claim). The 'Analysis' is the structural engineering that connects them. Without it, the reader is left to cross the gap themselves, which often leads to misinterpretation.

For the first practice moment, I'll present a paragraph that is 90% summary of a historical event. I want to guide the students in a 'search and destroy' mission for filler description. We will collectively highlight sentences that merely repeat known facts and brainstorm how to replace them with sentences that explain the *significance* of those facts. This reveals the 'weight' of their writing—if most of the paragraph can be deleted without losing the argument, the writing is too descriptive.

Finally, I will introduce the 'Three-Layer Analysis' model: Observation (the fact), Context (the surrounding circumstances), and Implication (the impact on the overall thesis). By visualizing these layers on the board, students can see that a truly analytical paragraph must touch all three. The session concludes with a challenge: rewriting a descriptive passage using at least three 'Strong Verbs' from our list. This final task ensures they transition from conceptual understanding to practical application, giving them the linguistic tools to enter professional academic discourse with authority.

tasks: Rewrite a descriptive paragraph into an analytical one using provided 'strong verbs'.
Identify and remove 'filler description' from a sample draft passage.

lectures.title: Counterargument
lectures.description: This lecture introduces the dialectical nature of academic writing, teaching you how to strengthen your own position by engaging with opposing viewpoints and avoiding logical errors.

sessions.title: Anticipating Objections
sessions.description: This session teaches you the 'imaginary critic' technique to find weaknesses in your own argument before a reader does. You will learn to identify common points of resistance and legitimate alternative perspectives, which is the first step toward creating a balanced and persuasive scholarly conversation. This habit of mind is essential for developing a mature, nuanced academic voice.
sessions.sessionOutline:
Start the session by challenging the 'monologue' mindset that many beginners bring to academic writing. In a concept-first public lecture style, visualize the essay not as a lecture delivered from a podium to a silent crowd, but as a person entering a room where a heated conversation is already happening. Use the whiteboard to draw a simple 'Triangle of Tension' between the Writer, the Subject, and the Skeptical Audience. Explain that the 'Skeptical Audience' isn't mean-spirited; they are simply well-informed peers who won't accept a claim just because it sounds confident. This sets the stage for the 'Imaginary Critic' technique: a mental exercise where we intentionally invite a critic to sit at our desk while we write. This shift is crucial because it transforms writing from a defensive act of proving oneself right into a collaborative act of seeking truth.

Introduce the 'Internal Devil's Advocate' framework to help students look for specific 'friction points' in their logic. On the board, map out three primary categories where resistance usually occurs: Evidence (Is the data old or biased?), Interpretation (Could this same data mean something else?), and Scope (Are we claiming this works for everyone when it only works for a few?). By categorizing objections this way, students move past the paralyzing fear that their 'whole argument is bad' and instead identify precise areas for reinforcement. Illustrate this with a relatable example, like a thesis claiming 'Remote work is universally better for productivity.' A critic would immediately point to the social isolation of new hires or the lack of mentorship for juniors. Identifying these isn't a failure—it’s an opportunity to sharpen the original claim.

Transition into a guided practice where students list three potential objections to a provided controversial thesis, such as 'Standardized testing should be abolished in university admissions.' The goal here is to reveal a common misconception: that admitting a weakness makes the argument weaker. On the contrary, explain that by naming the objection ourselves, we take control of the narrative. Use a whiteboard diagram of a 'fortress'—if you leave a back gate open, the critic will find it; if you stand at the gate and acknowledge the critic's presence, you demonstrate that you have already fortified your position. This exercise forces learners to step outside their own confirmation bias and look at their logic from the 'outside-in'.

Conclude by having students role-play the 'devil's advocate' for their own specific research projects. This is a diagnostic moment; if a student cannot think of a single objection to their claim, it usually means their claim is either a 'truism' (something everyone already agrees on) or it's too vague to be argued. Encourage them to ask themselves, 'What would my smartest opponent say is the biggest leap of faith I’m asking them to take?' This final reflection bridges the gap between abstract argumentation and the practical, nuanced voice required for professional scholarly output, emphasizing that a mature academic voice is built on the foundation of intellectual humility and rigorous self-questioning.

tasks: List three potential objections to a provided controversial thesis.
Role-play a 'devil's advocate' for your own project's main claim.

sessions.title: Conceding and Refuting
sessions.description: In this session, you will learn the linguistic templates for conceding a point ('While it is true that...') and refuting it ('Nonetheless...'). You will understand how acknowledging valid points from the opposition actually increases your own credibility (ethos).
